position_in_era.historical_role: The speed-variant heir: where Iron Man and the self-titled operate at funeral tempo, Paranoid proves the riff-first contract survives at double speed. The two-minute format demonstrates that the weight-first aesthetic is not tempo-dependent but structure-dependent — the riff governs even when the pace is punk-fast. First heavy metal song to chart in the UK top 5.

narrative_slots.production_facts: Recorded June 1970 at Regent Sound Studios. Written in approximately 25 minutes as a filler track when Rodger Bain needed two more minutes to complete the album. Iommi's riff in E minor descends at a pace double that of Iron Man. The song has no guitar solo — the riff IS the entire musical argument.
narrative_slots.member_dynamics: Ward reportedly composed the drum pattern in one pass. Butler's bass runs below Iommi's riff as pure support. Osbourne's vocal was written and recorded in a single session. The extreme speed of composition is reflected in the song's directness: there is no development, only riff statement and restatement.
narrative_slots.instrumentation_details: Iommi: Gibson SG; Butler: Fender Precision Bass; Ward: Ludwig drums; Osbourne: vocal. The song is in E minor, played at approximately 164 bpm — the fastest Sabbath recording to this point. No guitar solo or bridge.
narrative_slots.cultural_venue: UK #4 single, September 1970. The album Paranoid went to #1 UK Albums. The title track proved that heavy, riff-first music could be commercially dominant. The user (Vicky) holds a red heart for this track (id=16837172), making it the only anchor-era song in the red-heart collection.
narrative_slots.release_circumstances: The album title was changed from War Pigs to Paranoid after the single's success. The song's brevity and commercial success paradoxically helped establish that heavy metal was not exclusively album-format — the riff could work as a single.
